title: Delivering a Tough Message About Their Flaws Starts With Your Flaws
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article tackles the difficult task of confronting a team member's character flaws, noting that most people struggle to accept hard truths about themselves and become defensive when confronted directly. The recommended approach is for the leader to go first: naming their own flaws and struggles vividly before asking the team member, 'What about you?' This vulnerability, the author argues, disarms defensiveness by leveling the playing field rather than positioning the leader as judge. The piece acknowledges some team members will still resist recognizing their flaws, but frames the leader's own self-deprecation as the necessary first move in any productive version of this conversation.
points: Confronting a team member's character flaws directly tends to produce defensiveness and resistance.
Leaders can disarm that resistance by naming their own flaws and struggles first, before turning the question to the team member.
This self-deprecating opening levels the playing field rather than positioning the leader as sitting in judgment.
Even with this approach, some team members will still resist recognizing their own flaws -- but the conversation is more likely to land.
quotes: Some team members don’t know themselves well and fight the same demons on many days.
But making deep character flaws explicit, no matter how good a leader’s intentions might be, will often produce resistance and rejection.
They start with themselves. They point out their flaws and areas for development.
Then they turn to the team member and ask, “What about you?
By starting with themselves and admitting their flaws with a genuine vulnerability, leaders level the playing field and wipe away the defensiveness that undermines a productive conversation.
As in so many difficult situations, it starts with the leader.
